items.title: Lions get only 0.001% of the sun's energy that hit their grass
items.claim: Each trophic level passes about 10% of its energy to the next. Sun -> grass -> antelope -> lion. Three steps means lions retain 0.1% of grass energy. Add another step and you're down to 0.01%. The tenth-of-energy rule explains why food chains are short.

options.text: Most of the consumed energy goes to respiration (powering the consumer's metabolism), heat loss, and undigested waste; only a small fraction is converted into new tissue available to the next predator

items.reveal:
Raymond Lindeman (1942) measured energy flow in Cedar Bog Lake, Minnesota. He found progressive losses at each trophic level — formalising 'trophic efficiency'.

Typical values: primary producers fix ~1-2% of incident solar energy as net primary productivity. Herbivores extract ~10% of plant productivity. Carnivores ~10% of herbivore productivity. Top predators get a tiny fraction of the original solar input.

Consequences: food chains rarely exceed 4-5 trophic levels; predators have huge home ranges and small populations; ecosystems with apex predators are inherently fragile to disruption at the base.

The '10% rule' is an approximation. Efficiencies actually vary: ectotherms (fish, reptiles) can transfer 30-40% because they don't spend energy maintaining body heat. Endotherms (mammals, birds) burn most of what they eat to stay warm.

Vegetarian arguments often invoke this: feeding plants directly to people is ~10x more energy-efficient than routing them through livestock first.
items.why: Food chains feel boundless. Thermodynamics caps them at 4 or 5 links. Each predator carries the entropic cost of every prey it ate.

items.title: Reintroducing wolves changed the course of rivers in Yellowstone
items.claim: Grey wolves were exterminated from Yellowstone by 1926. In 1995, 14 wolves were reintroduced. Within 20 years, elk populations dropped, willows and aspen regrew along riverbanks, beaver populations rose, and river channels narrowed.

options.text: A trophic cascade: wolves reduce elk numbers and (especially) keep them moving, releasing browse pressure on streamside trees, which stabilise banks. The effect propagates through multiple trophic levels
Wolves drink large amounts of river water
It's coincidence — climate change did it

items.reveal:
The Yellowstone story is the textbook trophic cascade. Wolves don't only kill elk; they shift elk behaviour — herds avoid areas where they can't see predators coming, like valley bottoms with dense vegetation.

Released from constant browsing, willows and aspens regrow. Beavers, which need willows, return — by 2014, beaver colonies had increased from 1 to 9. Beaver dams trap sediment, raise water tables, create wetlands.

The full claim ('wolves changed the rivers') is contested. William Ripple and Robert Beschta documented the vegetation rebound; Arthur Middleton and others argue confounding factors (climate, bear predation, elk hunting outside the park) explain much of it.

What is uncontroversial: keystone species have effects on ecosystems vastly out of proportion to their biomass. Sea otters and kelp forests, starfish and intertidal communities, sharks and seagrass — similar cascades documented worldwide.

Keystone species concept: Robert Paine (1969), who removed starfish from a Pacific Northwest tide pool and watched it collapse to a mussel monoculture.
items.why: Ecosystems are imagined as bottom-up: plants determine herbivores determine carnivores. Top predators flip the picture — top-down control is real, and big effects can come from species with little biomass.

items.title: Wounded plants warn their neighbours via airborne chemicals
items.claim: An acacia tree being browsed by giraffes releases volatile chemicals (methyl jasmonate, ethylene). Downwind acacias detect the signal and produce defensive tannins within 30 minutes — before any herbivore has reached them.

options.text: The signal probably evolved for systemic intra-plant communication (alerting other parts of the same tree); the inter-plant 'warning' is likely a by-product, though it does benefit kin or close neighbours under some conditions
Plants control each other's defences telepathically
It's a coincidence, not a signal

items.reveal_title: Volatile organic compounds in plant communication
items.reveal:
Wouter van Hoven (1980s) and Edward Farmer/Clarence Ryan (1990s) showed that plants under attack release volatile signals that other plants detect.

Mechanism: damaged tissue produces jasmonic acid; some is released as methyl jasmonate (volatile). Other plants take it in through stomata. It triggers expression of defensive genes — protease inhibitors that make leaves indigestible, tannins, alkaloids.

Other signals include green leaf volatiles (the smell of cut grass), terpenoids, ethylene. Each can trigger specific responses in receivers.

The original function is almost certainly within-plant: signalling from damaged leaves to undamaged ones via volatile leakage through the air, faster than through phloem in some cases. Lab tests show same-individual leaves respond as well as neighbours' leaves do.

Some plants also send volatile signals that attract predators of their herbivores. Maize plants attacked by caterpillars release blends specific to the caterpillar species, attracting parasitic wasps that lay eggs in the caterpillars.

'Crying plant' studies are controversial. Effect sizes vary by experiment, and the term 'warning' is anthropomorphic — but the chemistry is real, well-characterised, and has agricultural implications (push-pull pest management exploits these signals).
items.why: Plants seem passive. Volatile chemical signalling is widespread, sophisticated, and rich — and entire chemical 'languages' between plants and their herbivores and predators are still being decoded.
